The missing HttpOnly flag enables this XSS-to-RCE chain — classified as Medium since it's a valid security concern that amplifies existing XSS vulnerabilities.

The download function reads the entire HTTP response with response.read() without any size limit. An attacker can provide a URL pointing to an extremely large file (or a slow-drip endpoint), causing memory exhaustion or resource starvation on the server. Classified as Low per DoS guidance — this is a generic DoS possibility through a normal endpoint that requires authentication to trigger.

The 'preferences' cookie is set via response.set_cookie() in toggle_darkmode (line 105) and after_request (line 127-128) without httponly=True. JavaScript can read and modify this cookie. Critically, the preferences cookie is deserialized using pickle.loads() in the before_request handler (line 118), so an XSS attack can replace the cookie with a malicious pickle payload to achieve remote code execution. The missing HttpOnly flag enables this XSS-to-RCE attack chain. Classified as Medium since it amplifies existing XSS vulnerabilities into RCE.

The 'preferences' cookie is set without secure=True in both toggle_darkmode (line 105) and after_request (line 127-128). This cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections (nginx only listens on port 80). Since the cookie is deserialized with pickle.loads(), a network attacker performing a MITM attack could modify the cookie in transit to inject a malicious pickle payload, achieving RCE. Classified as Low since it requires network-level attacker positioning, but the impact is amplified by the insecure pickle deserialization.

NOT VULNERABLE. The login query uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter method with a Python equality operator: session.query(User).filter(User.email == form.email.data). SQLAlchemy ORM automatically parameterizes these queries, preventing SQL injection. The email value is never interpolated into raw SQL.

NOT VULNERABLE. The user existence check uses SQLAlchemy ORM: session.query(session.query(User).where(User.email == form.email.data).exists()).scalar(). The ORM parameterizes the email comparison, preventing SQL injection despite the query involving user input.

NOT VULNERABLE. Passwords are properly hashed using bcrypt with a random salt: hashpw(form.password.data.encode('utf-8'), gensalt()). bcrypt is a strong, adaptive hashing algorithm suitable for password storage. The same secure pattern is used in account updates (routes/account.py:88).

NOT VULNERABLE. The search parameter is rendered in the input value attribute using Jinja2's default auto-escaping: value="{{search}}". Jinja2 automatically escapes HTML special characters (<, >, &, ") in template expressions, preventing attribute injection and reflected XSS in this context.

Reflected XSS: request.args.get('name') is passed to the template and rendered with {{ name | safe }}, disabling Jinja2 auto-escaping. Attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JS via the 'name' GET parameter: /sandbox/unsafe_params?name=<script>alert(1)</script>
Source of reflected XSS: request.args.get('name', 'world!') is passed unsanitized to render_template where it is rendered with | safe filter in the template

XSS via cookie or form input: {{ name | safe }} renders the 'name' variable (sourced from request.cookies.get('name') or request.form.get('name')) with escaping disabled. Exploitable via cookie manipulation or form submission.
Source of cookie/form-based XSS: request.cookies.get('name') and request.form.get('name') flow unsanitized into render_template where they are rendered with | safe filter

Stored XSS: {{ message.message | safe }} renders user-submitted feedback/message content with escaping disabled. Messages are stored in the database from user input (send_feedback endpoint or unauthenticated API POST) and displayed on the admin messages page, allowing XSS against admin users.

Stored XSS: {{ message.from_user | safe }} renders the from_user field with escaping disabled. The from_user field can be controlled directly via the unauthenticated API POST endpoint (from_user JSON field), enabling stored XSS against admin users viewing the messages page.

Stored XSS injection point: user-submitted feedback from request.form.get('feedback') is stored in Message model without sanitization. The message content is later rendered with | safe in admin/message.html.

Stored XSS injection point via unauthenticated API: message and from_user from JSON request body are stored in Message model without sanitization or authentication. Both fields are rendered with | safe in admin/message.html.

XSS via username: {{ g.user.username | safe }} renders the logged-in user's username with escaping disabled in the navbar. If a user can register with a username containing script tags, it will execute on every page. Exploitability depends on whether user registration exists (not in current code, but flask_admin ModelView for User may allow user creation by admin).

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY: 'Keep it secret, keep it safe'. This secret is used for signing session cookies. An attacker who knows this value can forge arbitrary session cookies, impersonate any user, and escalate privileges.

DEBUG mode enabled in production code: app.config['DEBUG'] = True exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which allows arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is known or guessable, and leaks stack traces, source code, and local variables to any user who triggers an error.

Plaintext password storage: User model stores passwords without any hashing. Passwords are stored as plain strings in the database (line 11: db.Column(db.String(200)), line 16: self.password = password). Anyone with database access can read all user passwords.

Password exposed in API serialization: User.serialize property includes the plaintext password field (line 27: 'password': self.password). This is used in the /api/v1/users/ endpoint, exposing all user passwords to anyone with API access.

API endpoint exposes all user passwords: UsersView.index() serializes all users including plaintext passwords via user.serialize. While admin_required decorator restricts access, the admin password itself is 'admin', making this easily exploitable.
Default admin password hardcoded as 'admin' (line 14: password='admin'). The admin user is created with trivially guessable credentials. The login page even displays 'admin/admin' as the credentials.

Open redirect: request.args.get('next') is passed directly to redirect() without any validation. An attacker can craft a URL like /toggle_xss_protection/?next=https://evil.com to redirect users to a malicious site.

Missing authentication on message creation API: MessagesView.post() has no @login_required or @admin_required decorator, allowing any unauthenticated user to submit messages. Combined with stored XSS in the admin message view, this allows unauthenticated attackers to inject XSS payloads targeting admin users.

X-XSS-Protection header explicitly set to 0 by default, disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter. While this header is deprecated in modern browsers, it actively removes a defense layer in older browsers.

Plaintext password comparison in authentication: user.password == password compares the submitted password directly against the stored plaintext password. No hashing algorithm is used, meaning passwords are stored and compared in cleartext.
New password stored in plaintext: the change_password endpoint stores the new password directly without hashing: User.query.filter_by(id=current_user.id).update({'password': new_password})

Plaintext password comparison in change_password handler: the current password is compared directly against the stored plaintext password (current_user.password == current_password) at line 26. This is distinct from flask-xss-020 (which covers the new password storage at lines 34-35) and flask-xss-019 (which covers login comparison at login/views.py:17). This is the current-password verification step in the change_password flow, confirming no hashing is used at any point.

Session fixation: login_user(user) is called without regenerating the session ID. Flask-Login does not automatically regenerate session IDs on login without explicit configuration. An attacker who can pre-set a session ID (e.g., via one of the existing XSS vulnerabilities or network access) can hijack the authenticated session after the victim logs in. The attack chain is realistic given the multiple XSS vulnerabilities already present in this application.

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint: no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism exists. Combined with plaintext password comparison (flask-xss-019) and a hardcoded default admin password of 'admin' (flask-xss-015), an attacker can perform unlimited brute-force login attempts with no throttling. This is especially dangerous given the trivially guessable default credentials.

IDOR via sequential integer IDs in UsersView.get(): the endpoint uses is_admin_or_owning_user(id) for authorization, but user IDs are sequential integers that can be easily enumerated. While the ownership check provides some protection, the predictable ID scheme enables user enumeration and probing attempts. The authorization check may be insufficient depending on implementation details.

Admin panel access control based on username string comparison: AdminOnlyMixin.is_accessible() delegates to is_admin_user(current_user), which checks if username equals 'admin'. This is a weak access control pattern — if any user can register or change their username to 'admin', they gain full admin panel access. This is the view-layer enforcement of the weak admin check defined in models.py (see flask-xss-028).

UsersView.get() exposes full user object including plaintext password: the single-user GET endpoint at line 84 returns the full user object via serialization. This is a distinct endpoint from the list-all-users endpoint already documented in flask-xss-014 (UsersView.index() at lines 71-75). Both use user.serialize which includes the plaintext password, but this is a separate code path and exposure point.

Full User object with plaintext password passed to every template context via g.user: the before_request handler assigns g.user = current_user, making the complete User model (including the plaintext password field) accessible in every template rendering context. While current templates don't directly render g.user.password, the data crosses a trust boundary into the template layer. This is the root injection point — distinct from flask-xss-009 (template rendering of username) and flask-xss-012/013 (model/API serialization).

Admin role determined by username string comparison: the is_admin property checks if username equals 'admin' rather than using a dedicated role or boolean field. If a user can register with the username 'admin' (or change their username to it), they gain admin privileges. No proper role-based access control exists. This is the model-layer definition that backs the admin panel access control in admin/views.py (see flask-xss-025).

Not vulnerable to SQL injection: User.query.filter_by(username=username) uses SQLAlchemy ORM which automatically parameterizes queries. User input from request.form.get('username') is safely bound as a parameter, not concatenated into SQL.
Not vulnerable: {{ page_name }} and {{ pages[page_name] }} use Jinja2 default auto-escaping (no | safe filter). Additionally, the values come from server-side URL rule parsing, not from user input.

Not vulnerable: {{ g.user.username }} and {{ g.user.email }} on the account area page use Jinja2 default auto-escaping (no | safe filter), so special characters in usernames or emails are properly HTML-escaped.

Not vulnerable to SQL injection: User.query.filter_by(id=current_user.id).update({'email': new_email}) uses SQLAlchemy ORM which parameterizes all values. The user-supplied email is safely bound as a parameter.
Not vulnerable to SQL injection: User.query.filter_by(id=user_id) uses SQLAlchemy ORM with parameterized queries. The user_id from Flask-Login's session is safely bound.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation. User-supplied username and password from request.form are directly embedded into the SQL query string: f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'". An attacker can bypass authentication or extract data with payloads like ' OR '1'='1' --.

Reflected XSS in search endpoint. The query parameter 'q' from request.args is directly interpolated into an HTML response via f-string: f"

Search Results for {query}

". No output encoding or escaping is applied. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the q parameter.

XSS via cookie value reflection. The 'session' cookie value (user-controllable) is embedded directly into the HTML response via f-string: f"

Welcome, {user}!

". An attacker who sets a malicious cookie value (or exploits the login to set it) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. The response also contains a hardcoded demonstrating the issue.

Hardcoded admin credentials at module level: USERNAME = 'admin' and PASSWORD = 'password123'. These credentials are embedded directly in source code, exposing them to anyone with access to the codebase.

Plaintext password storage. User credentials are inserted into the database without any hashing: INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('user1', 'password1'). The password column stores raw plaintext, allowing full credential compromise if the database is accessed.

The /dashboard endpoint has no authentication check. It reads a 'session' cookie but does not verify it against any session store or validate the user is authenticated. Any user can access the dashboard by navigating directly to /dashboard, defaulting to 'guest' if no cookie is set. There is no server-side session validation whatsoever.

Insecure session management via plain cookie. The session cookie is set with response.set_cookie('session', username) with no HttpOnly flag, no Secure flag, no SameSite attribute, and the value is the raw username (not a signed/encrypted session token). This allows cookie theft via XSS, session spoofing by setting arbitrary cookie values, and transmission over unencrypted connections.

The login form submits via POST to /login with no CSRF token. The Flask app does not use any CSRF protection middleware (e.g., Flask-WTF CSRFProtect). An attacker can craft a page that auto-submits the login form to perform login CSRF attacks.

The /login endpoint accepts POST requests with username/password without any rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection mechanism. The application uses weak hardcoded passwords ('password123', 'password1') and has no throttling on failed attempts. An attacker can perform unlimited credential guessing attempts. No Flask-Limiter or equivalent middleware is configured anywhere in the application.

The init_db function executes SQL statements with hardcoded string literals (CREATE TABLE and INSERT INTO with fixed values). No user input flows into these queries. Although the queries use string literals rather than parameterized queries, there is no injection vector because the values are compile-time constants, not user-controlled data.

The login failure response returns a static HTML string: 'Invalid credentials. Try again'. Although this is raw HTML returned from the endpoint, it contains no user-controlled input — the message is a hardcoded string literal. No XSS is possible because no user data is reflected in this response.

User-supplied 'ip' parameter from request.args is passed directly as an argument to subprocess.check_output(['ping', '-c', '4', ip]) without any validation or sanitization. While the list form prevents shell metacharacter injection, unsanitized input to a system command enables argument injection (e.g., passing flags like '-c 10000') and DNS-based attacks via attacker-controlled hostnames. Most SAST scanners will flag this as command injection.

Username ('admin') and password ('password123') are hardcoded as module-level constants USERNAME and PASSWORD, then used directly in the /login authentication check. Any attacker with source code access obtains valid credentials.

Untrusted data from request.data is passed directly to pickle.loads() at line 33. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server. The /unserialize endpoint accepts raw POST body and deserializes it without any validation.

User-supplied 'id' parameter from request.args is concatenated directly into a SQL query string: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '" + user_id + "'". This allows classic SQL injection. The query is then passed to run_query() which simulates database execution.

Flask application is run with debug=True (app.run(debug=True)). This enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger which exposes a Python REPL in the browser on unhandled exceptions, allowing arbitrary code execution. It also leaks detailed stack traces, source code, and environment variables to any user.

The /login endpoint at lines 19-26 accepts POST authentication requests with no rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection. This is distinct from the hardcoded credentials finding (CWE-798 at lines 16-17) as it enables network-based brute-force attacks independently of source code access. An attacker can send unlimited authentication attempts with no throttle, lockout, or delay applied at any point in the request handling.

Reflected XSS in the get_user function. The user-supplied 'id' parameter from request.args is concatenated into a SQL query string, passed to run_query() which returns 'Query result for: ' + query (embedding the unsanitized user input), and the result is returned via 'return str(result)'. Flask serves this with text/html content type by default, so an attacker can inject HTML/JavaScript via the id parameter (e.g., id=<script>alert(1)</script>) which will be rendered in the victim's browser. This is distinct from the SQL injection vulnerability (GT-004) at line 46 — both share the same unsanitized input but target different sinks (browser HTML rendering vs database query).

The requests.get() call uses a hardcoded URL ('https://example.com'), not user-controlled input. There is no SSRF vulnerability because the target URL cannot be influenced by an attacker. Scanners may flag the use of requests.get() but the destination is a static constant.

The run_query() function looks like it executes a SQL query but is actually a simulation that only performs string concatenation and returns the result as text. No actual database connection or query execution occurs — it simply returns 'Query result for: ' + query. The real SQL injection vulnerability is at line 46 where the query string is constructed with unsanitized input.

Path traversal via unsanitized 'p' GET parameter joined directly into file path: open(os.path.join(base_path, filename), 'rb').read(). An attacker can use '../../' sequences to read arbitrary files (e.g., ?p=../../settings.py to read Django settings including SECRET_KEY).

Arbitrary code execution via exec() on user-supplied base64-decoded POST data (Python 3 path): exec(base64.decodestring(bytes(first_name, 'ascii'))). Attacker can execute any Python code on the server.

Arbitrary code execution via exec() on user-supplied base64-decoded POST data (Python 2 fallback path): exec(base64.decodestring(first_name)). Same vulnerability as the Python 3 path but for Python 2 compatibility.

Reflected XSS via |safe filter on user-controlled 'qs' GET parameter in form input value attribute: value="{{qs|safe}}". Attacker can break out of the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript (e.g., qs=" onfocus=alert(1) autofocus x=").

Reflected XSS via |safe filter on URL path variable injected into JavaScript context: var myvar = "{{path|safe}}";. Attacker can break out of the string and execute arbitrary JavaScript by manipulating the URL path.
Reflected XSS via |safe filter on 'qs' GET parameter injected into JavaScript context: var myvar = "{{qs|safe}}";. Attacker can break out of the string and execute arbitrary JavaScript.

Reflected XSS via |safe filter on 'qs' GET parameter injected into JavaScript context: var x = "{{qs|safe}}";. This XSS is used in the CSRF exercise to demonstrate how XSS enables CSRF attacks via image tag injection.

Open redirect via unsanitized 'url' GET parameter passed directly to Django redirect(): return redirect(url). An attacker can craft a URL like ?url=http://evil.com to redirect users to a malicious site.

Unsafe function dispatch via globals().get(forward) using user-supplied 'fwd' GET parameter. An attacker can call any function in the module's global scope by name (e.g., ?fwd=admin to access the admin view, or ?fwd=boom to trigger errors). This is an unvalidated forward vulnerability.

Missing function-level access control. The admin page is served to anyone who passes ?action=admin in the GET parameter with no authentication or authorization check. Any user can access the admin template by simply adding the query parameter.

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). User profiles are accessed and modified by sequential numeric userid in URL (/direct-object-references/users/1, /users/2) with no authentication or authorization checks. Any user can view and modify any other user's profile data by changing the userid parameter.

DEBUG = True in production settings. This exposes detailed stack traces, SQL queries, template context, and settings values to any user who triggers an error. The boom() view at /misconfiguration/boom deliberately raises an exception to demonstrate this information disclosure.

Django SECRET_KEY is hardcoded in source code: 'h++jszpm)i@p%ay_b=cp#()^od!qns14)h%@qm3)p=cuo+st^a'. This key is used for cryptographic signing of sessions, CSRF tokens, and password reset tokens. Exposure allows session forgery and other attacks.

Global CSRF protection is disabled. The CsrfViewMiddleware is commented out in MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES: #'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware'. This means no views have CSRF protection, making all POST forms vulnerable to cross-site request forgery attacks.

View explicitly decorated with @csrf_exempt, additionally disabling any CSRF protection. Combined with the XSS vulnerability on the same page (|safe filter on qs parameter), this enables CSRF attacks via injected image tags to trigger gift card purchases.

Gift card purchase form with no CSRF token: <form method="POST"> without {% csrf_token %}. Combined with the globally disabled CSRF middleware, this form is vulnerable to cross-site request forgery attacks that could trigger unauthorized gift card purchases.

Django Debug Toolbar is enabled and can be activated by any user via ?debug=1 query parameter, debug POST field, or debug cookie. The toolbar exposes SQL queries, request/response headers, template context, settings, and other sensitive internal application details.

Intentional exception raise Exception('boom') in a view with DEBUG=True. This causes Django to display a full debug error page including the complete stack trace, settings (with SECRET_KEY), environment variables, and installed middleware to any user.
XFrameOptionsMiddleware is commented out: # 'django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware'. This allows the application to be framed by any origin, enabling clickjacking attacks.

The code_execution.html POST form lacks a {% csrf_token %} tag. With CSRF middleware globally disabled (settings.py), an attacker can forge a cross-origin POST request to the code execution endpoint, which passes submitted data to exec(base64.decode(POST['first_name'])). This enables CSRF-triggered remote code execution. The ground truth already tracks per-form CSRF omissions as distinct entries (e.g. gift_card.html in GT-016), and this form targets the most dangerous endpoint in the application (RCE via exec).

The SQL injection exercise POST form lacks a {% csrf_token %} tag. With CSRF middleware globally disabled in settings.py, this form has no CSRF protection at either the middleware or template layer. An attacker can forge cross-origin POST requests to this endpoint. Even if the middleware were re-enabled, the form would remain unprotected due to the missing token.

The xss_form view sets a cookie via response.set_cookie(key='monster', value='omnomnomnomnom!') without httponly=True. This makes the cookie accessible to JavaScript via document.cookie. Combined with the reflected XSS vulnerability on the same page (GT-004, |safe filter on qs parameter in form.html), an attacker can steal this cookie value through injected JavaScript.

The xss_form view sets a cookie via response.set_cookie(key='monster', value='omnomnomnomnom!') at line 100 without secure=True. The cookie will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, allowing interception by network attackers. This is a distinct issue from the missing HttpOnly flag (lets-be-bad-guys-022) on the same set_cookie call.

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is not set in settings.py (defaults to False). The session engine is configured at line 174 (SESSION_ENGINE = 'django.contrib.sessions.backends.cache') but session cookies will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, allowing interception by network attackers performing MITM or sniffing. This is a missing security hardening configuration rather than an explicit misconfiguration.

The sql() view contains SQL injection-looking strings ("SELECT id from Users where first_name = ''; DROP TABLE Users;--") but these are only used as display text for the exercise solution. No actual database query is executed — the strings are passed directly to the template for rendering. The view only compares user input against an expected answer string.

The 'fwd' parameter is displayed in {{ fwd }} but Django auto-escapes template variables by default (no |safe filter used). The output is placed inside a <code> tag and will be HTML-escaped, preventing XSS injection.

User input 'name' is rendered in an HTML input value attribute: <input name="name" value="{{ name }}">. While this looks like it could be XSS, Django's default auto-escaping will HTML-encode special characters (<, >, ", &), preventing attribute breakout and XSS injection.

The 'msg' variable is rendered with {{ msg }} in the template, which looks like it could allow XSS. However, the msg variable is set server-side to fixed strings ('That was worth trying...', 'You're on the right track...', 'Keep trying...') and is never directly user-controlled. Django's auto-escaping is also active.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of username and password into SQL query: query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'". Tainted data from form.username.data and form.password.data flows directly into conn.execute(query) at line 177 without parameterization.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of search_term into LIKE query: query = f"SELECT * FROM comments WHERE content LIKE '%{search_term}%'". User input from form.search.data flows directly into cursor.execute(query) at line 249.

Blind SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user_id into query: query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}". Integer input from form is interpolated without parameterization and executed at conn.execute(query) line 494. Supports time-based blind SQLi.

SSRF via user-supplied URL passed directly to requests.get(url, timeout=2) at line 384. No URL validation or allowlist. Attacker can make the server request internal resources (localhost, internal IPs, cloud metadata endpoints). Response content is returned to the user (up to 500 chars).

Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads() on user-supplied base64-decoded data at line 436. User provides base64-encoded data through a form, which is decoded and passed to pickle.loads(decoded). This allows arbitrary code execution via crafted pickle payloads (e.g., __reduce__ method).

DOM-based XSS via innerHTML assignment with unsanitized URL hash data. At line 139-143: the hash fragment is parsed with URLSearchParams, the 'message' parameter is extracted, and directly assigned via document.getElementById('message').innerHTML = message. No sanitization (e.g., DOMPurify) is applied.

IDOR vulnerability in /profile/<int:user_id> endpoint. Any authenticated user can access any other user's profile by changing the user_id parameter in the URL. The route fetches and displays the target user's data (username, email, role) without verifying that the requesting user has permission to view that profile.

BOLA/IDOR in /api/user/<int:user_id> API endpoint. Any authenticated user can retrieve any other user's data (id, username, email, role) by enumerating user IDs. The endpoint returns full user details including a CTF flag when accessing another user's data, confirming the authorization bypass.

Unrestricted file upload at /upload endpoint. Files are saved to static/uploads/ with only os.path.basename() sanitization on the filename (line 320). No file type validation, content-type checking, or extension allowlist is enforced before saving (line 322). Malicious files like .php webshells can be uploaded and served via /uploads/<filename>. Additionally, CSRF protection is explicitly disabled (@csrf.exempt at line 304).

CSRF vulnerability on /csrf endpoint due to @csrf.exempt decorator at line 538 which disables Flask-WTF CSRF protection. The endpoint allows email updates via POST without CSRF token validation. An attacker can craft a malicious page that auto-submits a form to change the victim's email. Exploit pages are provided at /csrf-exploit and /malicious-csrf-exploit.

CSRF vulnerability on /upload endpoint due to @csrf.exempt decorator at line 304 which disables Flask-WTF CSRF protection. An attacker can craft a malicious page that uploads arbitrary files on behalf of a logged-in victim.

CSRF vulnerability on /transfer endpoint via GET request. The transfer route accepts GET requests with an 'amount' parameter (line 276) and processes state-changing transfers without CSRF validation. GET requests bypass Flask-WTF CSRF protection. The malicious_csrf_example.html demonstrates this exploit with an auto-submitting form.

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'secure-secret-key-12345'. This key is used for session signing. An attacker who knows this key can forge session cookies, leading to authentication bypass and session hijacking.

Hardcoded default credentials with plaintext passwords in database initialization. admin/password (line 96-97) and user2/password2 (line 98-99) are inserted with plaintext passwords. No hashing (bcrypt, argon2, etc.) is applied. These weak credentials allow trivial authentication bypass.

Plaintext credentials stored in an accessible file: admin:admin123 and user1:password123. This file is within the application directory and could be served if directory listing is enabled or path traversal is possible.

Flask debug mode enabled in production: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, debug=True). Debug mode exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger which allows arbitrary code execution on the server. Combined with host='0.0.0.0', this is accessible from any network interface.

Database error details exposed to user: error = f"Database error: {str(e)}". The raw exception message from SQLite is displayed to the user, potentially revealing table structure, column names, and query syntax that aids SQL injection attacks.

Executed SQL query is displayed to the user via the executed_query variable passed to the login template at line 206. This reveals the full SQL query including injected payloads, aiding attackers in refining SQL injection attacks.

The /api/flag endpoint returns sensitive data (flag{flask_api_vuln}) without any authentication check. Unlike other routes that verify 'user' in session, this endpoint is accessible to unauthenticated users.

Predictable session token generation: predictable_session_id = f"{user['username'].lower()}_auth_123". Session IDs follow a trivially guessable pattern (username + '_auth_123'). An attacker can compute any user's session ID knowing only their username, enabling session hijacking.

Insecure cookie set without security flags: response.set_cookie('vuln_session_id', predictable_session_id). The cookie is set without httponly=True (accessible to JavaScript/XSS), without secure=True (sent over HTTP), and without samesite attribute (vulnerable to CSRF). Combined with the predictable session ID value, this enables session hijacking.

SQL error details exposed to user in comment search: error = f"Error executing query: {str(e)}". Raw SQLite exception messages are displayed, revealing database schema information that aids SQL injection exploitation.

Sensitive flag file (flag{flask_hidden_flag}) stored in the hackable/ directory within the application. If directory listing or path traversal vulnerabilities are exploited, this file exposes sensitive data.

The /comments-log endpoint reads and returns the contents of static/comments.txt without any authentication check. No session verification is performed, allowing unauthenticated access to potentially sensitive comment data.

Hardcoded database credentials (username 'root', password 'examplePW') in a PHP file stored in the publicly accessible static/uploads/ directory. While the Flask application does not execute PHP, the file is served statically and its contents (including credentials) are readable by anyone who can access the URL. This is distinct from GT-009 (unrestricted file upload) which covers the upload mechanism, not the credential exposure within uploaded files.

The login endpoint at /login (lines 152-206) has no rate limiting, allowing unlimited authentication attempts. No Flask-Limiter or equivalent protection is applied. Combined with the existing SQL injection vulnerability (GT-001) and weak/plaintext passwords (GT-014), this makes brute force and credential stuffing attacks trivial. An attacker can submit unlimited login requests without any throttling or lockout.

The login handler prints the full SQL query including the user-supplied plaintext password to stdout/server logs via print(f"Executing: {query}"). This is distinct from GT-018 (which covers the executed query being displayed to the user via template rendering at line 166/206). This finding concerns server-side logging of credentials — any operator, log aggregation system, or attacker with log access can harvest user passwords in plaintext from application logs.

The reset endpoint for comments (lines 644-645) executes DELETE FROM comments without scoping to the authenticated user, allowing any authenticated user to delete ALL comments system-wide. There is no ownership check or admin privilege verification before the bulk deletion. This is a missing function-level authorization check — a real broken access control vulnerability not covered by existing ground truth entries.

The log_action function writes user-controlled data (user, action, details parameters) directly into the logs database table without sanitization. Multiple callers pass user-controlled input into the details field (e.g., DOM XSS payload, transfer amounts). An attacker can inject misleading log entries to tamper with audit trails, and if logs are rendered in an admin interface, this could enable stored XSS. The same function is also defined in database.py (lines 141-147) — both represent the same root cause.

NOT VULNERABLE to XXE. Although ET.fromstring(xml_data) at line 409 parses user-supplied XML, Python's xml.etree.ElementTree does NOT resolve external entities by default. The app checks for '<!ENTITY' in the input string (line 405) as a pattern-matching challenge detection, but the actual XML parser cannot fetch external resources. External entity payloads will fail silently or error. This is safe against XXE (CWE-611).

NOT VULNERABLE to SSTI. The ssti() function uses render_template('ssti.html', ..., name=name) at line 536, NOT render_template_string(). Jinja2's render_template passes variables to a pre-compiled template. The template renders {{ name }} which outputs the variable's value as text - it does NOT interpret the value as template code. User input containing {{ 7*7 }} would be displayed literally (and HTML-escaped), not evaluated to 49. The app's pattern check ('{{' in name) at line 532 is challenge detection only.

NOT VULNERABLE to reflected XSS via server-side rendering. The query parameter from request.args.get('query') is passed to render_template at line 461 as query=query. In reflected_xss.html:74, {{ query }} is rendered with Jinja2's default auto-escaping which HTML-encodes special characters (<, >, ", &). The template also has {{ search | safe }} at line 56, but 'search' is NOT passed in the template context (only 'query', 'success', 'error' are), so it resolves to an empty string. No actual XSS is possible through the server-side rendering path.

NOT VULNERABLE. Dashboard queries use parameterized queries with ? placeholders: conn.execute("SELECT * FROM progress WHERE user = ?", (session['user'],)) at line 213 and conn.execute("SELECT * FROM logs WHERE user = ? ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 5", (session['user'],)) at line 214. The session['user'] value is passed as a parameter, not interpolated into the query string.

NOT VULNERABLE to SQL injection. The profile endpoint uses a parameterized query: conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)) at line 345. The user_id is passed as a parameter via Flask's int URL converter (<int:user_id>), which also ensures type safety. Note: the endpoint IS vulnerable to IDOR (documented separately) but NOT to SQL injection.

NOT VULNERABLE to SQL injection. The API user endpoint uses a parameterized query: conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)) at line 613. The user_id parameter is type-checked by Flask's int URL converter. Note: the endpoint IS vulnerable to BOLA/IDOR (documented separately) but NOT to SQL injection.
SQL injection via string concatenation in raw query: sql_query = "SELECT * FROM introduction_login WHERE user='"+name+"' AND password='"+password+"'", then passed to login.objects.raw(sql_query)
SQL injection via string concatenation: sql_query = "SELECT * FROM introduction_sql_lab_table WHERE id='"+name+"'AND password='"+password+"'", then passed to sql_lab_table.objects.raw(sql_query)
Reflected XSS via |safe filter on user-controlled query parameter: {{query|safe}} renders unsanitized GET parameter 'q' directly into HTML
Reflected XSS via |safe filter on POST parameter 'username': {{ username|safe }}. The server-side filter only strips tags but can be bypassed with other HTML tags (e.g., )

XSS in script context: user-controlled 'code' variable is rendered inside a <script> tag as {{code}}. The server strips alphanumeric characters but allows special characters like []()!+ enabling JSFuck-style XSS payloads
Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads() on user-controlled cookie 'token': base64-decoded cookie data is passed directly to pickle.loads(token), enabling arbitrary code execution
XXE vulnerability: XML parser created with feature_external_ges set to True, then parses user-supplied request body. This enables external entity resolution for file read and SSRF attacks

OS command injection: user-supplied 'domain' POST parameter is formatted into shell command (e.g., 'nslookup {}' or 'dig {}') and executed via subprocess.Popen with shell=True. URL stripping is insufficient; command separators like ; or && still work
Arbitrary code execution via eval(): user-supplied 'val' POST parameter is passed directly to Python eval() without any sanitization, enabling arbitrary code execution
Broken authentication via weak OTP: OTP is only 3 digits (100-999), easily brute-forceable. For non-admin users, the OTP is returned directly in the response. No rate limiting on OTP verification
Broken access control via client-side cookie: admin access is granted when request.COOKIES.get('admin') == '1'. An attacker can simply set this cookie to gain admin privileges and access secret data
Broken access control via client-side cookie: admin access is granted when request.COOKIES.get('admin') == '1', identical to ba_lab. Attacker can forge the admin cookie
Broken access control via User-Agent header: admin access is granted when user_agent == 'pygoat_admin'. An attacker can simply set User-Agent header to gain admin privileges

Missing authorization check: the secret endpoint at /broken_access_controle/secret has no authorization check beyond basic authentication. Any authenticated user can access admin-only secret content by directly navigating to the URL

Path traversal via user-controlled file path: POST parameter 'blog' is joined with dirname and opened directly with open(filename,'r'). Attacker can use ../ sequences to read arbitrary files on the server
SSRF via requests.get(): user-supplied 'url' POST parameter is passed directly to requests.get(url) without any URL validation or allowlist, enabling requests to internal services

Server-side template injection: user-supplied 'blog' POST content is written directly into a Django template file and later rendered. The filter_blog function does no sanitization (returns input unchanged). Attacker can inject Django template tags for code execution

Insecure YAML deserialization: user-uploaded YAML file is parsed with yaml.load(file, yaml.Loader) using the unsafe Loader class, enabling arbitrary Python code execution via YAML deserialization gadgets
Code injection via PIL ImageMath.eval(): user-supplied 'function' POST parameter is passed directly to ImageMath.eval(function_str, ...) which can execute arbitrary Python expressions
Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY in settings: SECRET_KEY = 'lr66%-a!$km5ed@n5ug!tya5bv!0(yqwa1tn!q%0%3m2nh%oml'. This key is used for cryptographic signing and session management
Debug mode enabled in production: DEBUG = True exposes detailed error pages with stack traces, settings, and environment variables to attackers
Sensitive data hardcoded in settings: SENSITIVE_DATA = 'FLAGTHATNEEDSTOBEFOUND' is a flag stored in plaintext in the settings file
Weak hardcoded JWT secret key: SECRET_COOKIE_KEY = 'PYGOAT' used for signing JWT tokens in sec_misconfig_lab3, trivially guessable

CSRF vulnerability: the money transfer endpoint is decorated with @csrf_exempt, disabling Django's CSRF protection. Combined with the GET-based transfer API at csrf_transfer_monei_api, this allows cross-site request forgery to transfer funds

State-changing operation via GET request: money transfer is performed via GET request to /mitre/9/lab/api/<recipient>/<amount>, enabling CSRF attacks via simple link or image tag. No CSRF token validation
Arbitrary code execution via eval(): user-supplied 'expression' POST parameter is passed directly to eval(expression) without any sanitization
OS command injection: user-supplied 'ip' POST parameter is concatenated into 'nmap ' + ip and executed via subprocess.Popen with shell=True in command_out(). No input validation or sanitization
Hardcoded JWT secret: jwt.encode(payload, 'csrf_vulneribility', algorithm='HS256') uses a weak, hardcoded secret key for JWT token signing
Weak password hashing using MD5: password = md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() — MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage
Weak password hashing using MD5: password = md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() — MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage

Privilege escalation via plaintext cookie manipulation: the cookie format is 'username|expiry' in plaintext. Changing the username part to 'admin' grants admin access. No integrity protection (HMAC/signature) on the cookie

IDOR via sequential userid cookie: login is performed by reading an integer userid from cookies (request.COOKIES['userid']) and looking up the user. An attacker can iterate through userid values to access other users' accounts
Plaintext password storage: user password is stored directly without hashing in authLogin.objects.create(name=name, username=user_name, password=passwd)

Security misconfiguration: access control based on X-Host header which is client-controlled. Setting X-Host to 'admin.localhost:8000' bypasses the check and reveals the secret key. The XHost value is also reflected in the response without sanitization

Arbitrary file write / code injection: user-supplied 'log_code' and 'api_code' POST parameters are written directly to Python source files (playground/A9/main.py and playground/A9/api.py) which are then imported and executed
Arbitrary file write: user-supplied 'code' POST parameter is written directly to playground/A6/utility.py Python source file without sanitization
Arbitrary file write: user-supplied Python code is transformed and written to playground/ssrf/main.py which is imported and executed by the application
Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads(): user-supplied base64-encoded data from POST form is decoded and passed to pickle.loads(decoded_data), enabling arbitrary code execution
Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.secret_key = 'your-secret-key-here' is a trivially guessable secret key used for session signing
Hardcoded plaintext credentials: admin/admin123 and user/password123 passwords stored in plaintext in source code
Insecure session token: session token is created by base64-encoding 'username:timestamp', trivially decodable and forgeable. No cryptographic integrity protection
Plaintext password storage: registered users' passwords are stored in plaintext in the users dictionary: 'password': password
Debug mode enabled: app.run(debug=True) enables Flask debug mode with interactive debugger, potentially allowing RCE via the Werkzeug debugger console

Password reset token exposed in response: the reset token is returned directly to the user via flash message instead of being sent to the email address, allowing any user who knows an email to reset that account's password

Missing authentication and authorization: the /api/all-users/ endpoint exposes all users' sensitive data (credit cards, SSNs, API keys) without any authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access all data
Sensitive data exposure via API: the /api/user-data/ endpoint returns full credit card number, SSN, and API key in plaintext JSON without masking
Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY: SECRET_KEY = 'django-insecure-key-for-demonstration-only' is trivially guessable and labeled as insecure
Debug mode enabled: DEBUG = True in production settings exposes detailed error pages
Overly permissive ALLOWED_HOSTS: ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*'] allows the application to serve requests from any hostname, enabling host header attacks
Hardcoded credentials in source code: username 'jack' with password 'jacktheripper' is hardcoded in the access control lab view
Hardcoded credentials: username 'John'/'reaper' and 'admin'/'admin_pass' are hardcoded in the view
Sensitive data stored in plaintext: credit card numbers, SSNs, and API keys are stored as plain CharField without encryption in the database model
Unsafe subprocess execution: subprocess.Popen(command, shell=True, ...) accepts arbitrary command strings with shell=True, called from mitre_lab_17_api with user input
NOT vulnerable: login.objects.filter(user=name) uses Django ORM's parameterized query, which safely escapes user input. This is the existence check before the vulnerable raw query
NOT vulnerable: {{company}}, {{ceo}}, {{about}} are rendered without |safe filter, so Django's auto-escaping protects against XSS. Values come from database but are properly escaped on output

NOT vulnerable: pickle.dumps(TestUser()) serializes a server-controlled dataclass instance. The serialized default token is created at module load time with known data, not from user input. The vulnerability is in the deserialization at line 214, not here
NOT vulnerable: login.objects.filter(user=user, password=password) uses Django ORM's parameterized queries, not raw SQL. Despite accepting user input, the ORM safely handles parameterization

NOT vulnerable in HTML context: {{code}} on line 19 is rendered in

tags without |safe, so Django auto-escaping prevents XSS in the HTML context. The vulnerability exists in the script context on line 22, but not here

NOT a real credential exposure: USER_A7_LAB3 contains SHA-256 hashed passwords (not plaintext). These are intentionally hardcoded demo data for the authentication failure lab, and passwords are properly hashed before comparison
NOT vulnerable: {{balance}} is rendered without |safe, so Django auto-escaping applies. The balance value comes from the database as an integer, providing no XSS vector

NOT a real exposure: FLAG = 'NOT_SUPPOSED_TO_BE_ACCESSED' is a constant defined in Python code that is never rendered in any response or template. It exists as target data for educational purposes but is not directly exposed through any endpoint

NOT directly exploitable SSRF: this function reads local files using os.path.join, which is a path traversal issue, but it is only called internally from the SSRF code checker test bench (apis.py:ssrf_code_checker) with controlled inputs, not directly from user requests

NOT vulnerable to brute force: auth_failure_lab2 uses argon2 PasswordHasher for verification and implements account lockout after 5 failed attempts with a 24-hour cooldown period. This is the 'secure' version of the auth lab

Sensitive PII (full credit card number, full SSN, API key) rendered in HTML comments using Django template variables {{ user_data.credit_card }}, {{ user_data.ssn }}, {{ user_data.api_key }}. HTML comments are visible to anyone viewing page source.

Reflected XSS via |safe filter on user-controlled GET parameter 'username': {{username | safe}} disables Django auto-escaping, allowing injection of arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. The form on line 16 uses method='get' with name='username'.

Predictable password reset token generated using MD5 hash of email concatenated with timestamp: token = hashlib.md5(f"{email}:{datetime.now()}".encode()).hexdigest(). MD5 is weak and the timestamp is predictable, allowing an attacker to brute-force the reset token.

API keys generated using Python's non-cryptographic random module: random.choices(chars, k=16) with only lowercase + digits (36 chars). The Mersenne Twister PRNG is predictable if seed or enough output is known. Code comment acknowledges weakness.

API key exposed in client-side JavaScript variable and stored in localStorage: localStorage.setItem('user_api_key', "{{ user_data.api_key }}"). Accessible via XSS, browser extensions, dev tools, and persists across sessions.
User password logged in plaintext: L.info(f"POST request with username {username} and password {password}") writes credentials to log file, exposing them to anyone with log access.
Hardcoded credentials: if username == "admin" and password == "admin" used for authentication. Trivially guessable admin/admin credentials in a @csrf_exempt endpoint.

DOM XSS via innerHTML: li.innerHTML = data.logs[i] inserts log data directly into DOM. Log entries contain user-controlled content (usernames, passwords from POST requests logged in api.py), allowing script injection through crafted log entries.

XSS via |safe filter on SSRF response content: {{response | safe}} renders the fetched URL's content without escaping. An attacker can point the SSRF to a URL returning malicious HTML/JavaScript, which will be rendered in the victim's browser.

DOM XSS via innerHTML in nmap results: output.innerHTML += "" + ports[p] + "
" inserts nmap API output into DOM without sanitization. Since the nmap command is constructed from user input via command injection (mitre_lab_17_api), attacker-crafted output could contain malicious HTML/JavaScript.

Weak password hashing: customHash uses SHA-256 with string reversal (hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()[::-1]). SHA-256 without salt or key stretching is fast to brute-force; reversing the hex digest adds no cryptographic strength.

SQL query structure exposed in error template: {{ sql_error }} renders the raw SQL query to the user on failed login attempts, revealing table names, column names, and query structure that aids SQL injection attacks.

No rate limiting or account lockout on login endpoint. Unlimited authentication attempts allowed, enabling brute-force attacks against accounts that protect sensitive PII (credit cards, SSNs, API keys).
JWT authentication cookie 'auth_cookiee' set without HttpOnly flag: response.set_cookie('auth_cookiee', cookie) makes the JWT token accessible to JavaScript, enabling theft via XSS attacks.

Log injection via unsanitized user input: logging.warning/info/error calls include user-controlled 'user' (from POST) and 'ip' (from X-Forwarded-For header) without newline sanitization, enabling log forging and audit trail corruption.

HTML comments reveal access control bypass method: comments disclose that admin access is controlled by User-Agent header value 'pygoat_admin', directly enabling exploitation of pygoat-013 (broken access control via User-Agent).

Log injection via unsanitized messages: the Log class writes user-controlled data (including usernames and passwords from POST requests at line 16) directly to log file without sanitizing newline characters, enabling log forging.

SQL injection via string concatenation: db.execute('SELECT pageId, title, content FROM pages WHERE pageId='+pageId). The pageId parameter comes directly from the URL path /dashboard/<pageId> without any sanitization or parameterization.

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via the 404 error handler. The request URL is inserted into a template string using Python .format() on line 94, then passed to render_template_string() on line 95. An attacker can inject Jinja2 template expressions (e.g., {{7*7}}) into the URL, achieving RCE. Combined with the system_call context processor from Monitoring.py, this enables direct OS command execution via {{system_call('id')}}.

Insecure pickle deserialization. User-supplied hex-encoded data from request.form['data_obj'] is decoded, written to a file, then loaded with pickle.load() on line 27. Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution via crafted __reduce__ methods.

Insecure YAML deserialization. User-supplied base64-encoded input from the URL path is decoded and passed to yaml.load() without specifying a safe Loader (line 18). With pyyaml 3.13 (from requirements.txt), yaml.load() uses the full Loader by default, allowing arbitrary Python object instantiation and code execution via !!python/object tags.

Reflected XSS via disabled autoescaping. The search parameter from user input is rendered in the template with {% autoescape false %}{{search}}{% endautoescape %} on line 13. The controller (Search.py:9-10) passes the raw request.form.get('search') value directly to the template. Additionally, X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to '0' in the controller.

XML External Entity (XXE) injection. User-supplied XML from request.form['customers'] is parsed by xml.dom.pulldom.parseString() on line 15 without disabling external entity resolution. This allows an attacker to read local files, perform SSRF, or cause DoS via entity expansion.

Path traversal / arbitrary file read. The fileName parameter from request.form['example_file'] (line 29) is used directly in open() (line 30) and send_file() (line 31) without any path validation. An attacker can supply paths like '../../../../etc/passwd' to read arbitrary files from the server.

Path traversal in file upload. The uploaded filename (file.filename) is used directly in file.save('uploads/'+filename) on line 48 without sanitization via werkzeug.utils.secure_filename(). An attacker can craft a filename containing '../' sequences to write files to arbitrary locations on the server. Although extension checking exists via allowed_file(), the filename itself is not sanitized for directory traversal.

OS command execution via os.popen(). The system_call function on line 13 executes arbitrary OS commands via os.popen(command).read(). This function is registered as a Jinja2 context processor available to ALL templates. While the monitoring template uses hardcoded commands, the SSTI vulnerability in the 404 handler allows an attacker to invoke {{system_call('arbitrary_command')}} for full RCE.

Hardcoded admin credentials. The login function checks password == 'admin' and username == 'admin' on line 12, exposing plaintext credentials in source code. Anyone with access to the source can authenticate as admin.

Hardcoded weak Flask SECRET_KEY set to 'random' on line 5. Flask uses SECRET_KEY to cryptographically sign session cookies. A known/weak secret key allows an attacker to forge session cookies, bypass authentication, and impersonate any user.

Flask debug mode enabled in production (app.debug = True on line 6). This exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which allows arbitrary Python code execution in the browser. It also exposes detailed stack traces, environment variables, and source code to attackers.

Authentication bypass via /webmaster endpoint. The obscurity() function sets session['loggedin'] to a random UUID on line 12 without any authentication check. Any unauthenticated user visiting /webmaster gets a valid session, bypassing the login requirement for protected endpoints like /confidential, /validator, and /monitoring.

Overly permissive CORS configuration. CORS is configured with origins='*' on line 8, allowing any domain to make cross-origin requests to the application. Combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true set in Confidential.py, this enables cross-origin credential theft attacks against authenticated users.

Stored XSS via javascript: URL in messaging link. User-supplied link data is stored in the database and rendered as href="{{item[3]}}" on line 56. While Jinja2 autoescaping prevents HTML injection, it does NOT prevent javascript: protocol URLs. An attacker can submit 'javascript:alert(document.cookie)' as the link value, and any user clicking 'Check Source' will execute the attacker's JavaScript.

Plaintext credentials exposed in HTML template. The webmaster page displays usernames and passwords in an HTML table (lines 23-41): Mark/Thisismysecretpass, Jacob/BirdLover1, Larry/Letmein123. These credentials are accessible to any user who can reach the /webmaster endpoint, which requires no authentication.

Weak password hashing. User passwords are stored as unsalted MD5 hashes (lines 15-18), e.g., '0cef1fb10f60529028a71f58e54ed07b' for Admin. MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsalted hashes are trivially reversible via rainbow tables. Passwords should use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2 with unique salts.

Information disclosure via monitoring page. The template executes and displays the output of system commands: 'ps aux | grep 8081' (line 10) and 'cat /etc/passwd' (line 22). This exposes process listing and system user accounts to any user who can access the /monitoring endpoint.

X-XSS-Protection header explicitly disabled. The Search controller sets X-XSS-Protection to '0' on line 11, disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter. This actively removes a defense layer, making the reflected XSS vulnerability on this endpoint easier to exploit.

Access-Control-Allow-Credentials set to true on the confidential data endpoint (line 10). Combined with the wildcard CORS origin in runserver.py, this allows malicious third-party sites to make authenticated cross-origin requests and steal the confidential salary data returned by this endpoint.

False positive: parameterized SQL query. The storeMessages function uses parameterized placeholders (?) on line 13: db.execute('INSERT INTO messages(name, message, link, timestamp)VALUES(?,?,?,?)', (name, message, link, ...)). Despite accepting user-controlled name, message, and link parameters, the use of parameterized queries prevents SQL injection.

False positive: SQL query with no user input. The getMessages function on line 8 executes a static query 'SELECT messageId, name, message, link, timestamp FROM messages' with no user-controlled parameters. Although it constructs a SQL string, no external input can influence the query.

False positive: autoescaped template output. The messaging template renders user-supplied name ({{item[1]}} on line 47) and message ({{item[2]}} on line 52) from the database. Although this is user-controlled data, Jinja2's default autoescaping is enabled (no autoescape false block), so HTML special characters are escaped, preventing XSS through these output points.

False positive: pickle.load on locally-generated data. The /about GET handler (start function) serializes a hardcoded dictionary on line 12-13 and immediately deserializes it on lines 14-15. The pickle file is generated server-side from trusted data — no user input influences the serialized content at this code path. The vulnerable deserialization is in the separate /about/sync POST handler.

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2. User-controlled 'name' query parameter is interpolated into an f-string on line 38 to build 'content', which is then passed to Template(content).render() on line 41. An attacker can inject Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., ?name={{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}) to achieve Remote Code Execution. The TODO in test_main.py lines 39-42 confirms this is an intentional vulnerability.

Reflected XSS via the 'name' query parameter. The user-supplied name value is directly interpolated into HTML content via f-string: content = f"

Hello, {name}!

..." with no HTML escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript (e.g., ?name=). The response_class=HTMLResponse ensures the browser renders the injected content.

Reflected XSS via the public_ip value. The response from the external PUBLIC_IP_SERVICE_URL is embedded unescaped into the HTML content via f-string: content = f"...{public_ip}...". If the external service returns malicious content (or is attacker-controlled via SSRF/env manipulation), arbitrary JavaScript can be injected into the page.

Server-Side Request Forgery. The PUBLIC_IP_SERVICE_URL is loaded from an environment variable (config.py line 11) with no URL validation or allowlist. requests.get(config.PUBLIC_IP_SERVICE_URL) is called on every request to the root endpoint. If an attacker can influence this environment variable (e.g., via container orchestration misconfiguration or .env file manipulation), they can force the server to make requests to arbitrary internal or external URLs.

Hardcoded secret token. SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN = '5u93R53Cr3tT0k3n' is hardcoded in source code with a FIXME comment indicating it should be loaded from an environment variable. This token value is committed to version control and visible to anyone with repository access.

Debug mode enabled in production. FastAPI is initialized with debug=config.DEBUG, where DEBUG is controlled by an environment variable that defaults to False. When DEBUG is set to true, FastAPI will return detailed stack traces and error information to clients, potentially exposing internal paths, code structure, and sensitive data.

WAF rules are defined but disabled. The Coraza WAF configuration has 'SecRuleEngine Off' on line 13, which means all subsequent security rules (SSTI blocking rule 1001, SQL injection rule 1002, XSS rule 1003, directory traversal rule 1004) are completely inactive. This renders the WAF ineffective despite appearing to provide protection.

Hardcoded default name. SUPER_SECRET_NAME = 'John Ripper' is hardcoded instead of being loaded from an environment variable (the os.getenv call is commented out with FIXME). While the name itself is not a credential, the 'SUPER_SECRET' prefix and FIXME comment indicate it was intended to be secret configuration.

The 'name' query parameter on line 19 is a string default parameter for the endpoint. Although it comes from user input (query string), it is only used in string interpolation for HTML output — it is NOT used as a URL target for requests.get(). The SSRF risk is in config.PUBLIC_IP_SERVICE_URL (an environment variable), not in the user-supplied 'name' parameter. A scanner might incorrectly flag user input flowing to requests.get(), but the name parameter does not reach that sink.

The DEBUG configuration on line 9 safely defaults to False. The expression os.getenv('DEBUG', 'False').lower() in ('true', '1', 'yes', 'y') correctly parses the environment variable with a safe default. Debug mode is only enabled if explicitly set via environment variable — the default behavior is secure.

User-controlled 'username' query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string via Jinja2.from_string('Welcome ' + username + '!'). An attacker can inject Jinja2 template expressions (e.g., {{ 7*7 }}, {{ config }}, or RCE payloads like {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}) which will be evaluated server-side. This allows arbitrary code execution.

The Jinja2 Environment is created with default settings (autoescape=False). User input from the 'username' query parameter is concatenated into the template string and the rendered output is returned as HTMLResponse. An attacker can inject HTML/JavaScript (e.g., <script>alert(1)</script>) which will be rendered in the victim's browser. Note: this is technically a consequence of the SSTI, but XSS is independently exploitable even without template syntax — plain HTML tags in the username are passed through to the HTML response.

The commented-out safe implementation on line 17 uses Jinja2 template variable interpolation: Jinja2.from_string('Welcome {{ user_name }}!').render(user_name=username). This passes user input as a template variable rather than concatenating it into the template string, so Jinja2 template expressions in the input would be treated as literal text, not evaluated. This is the correct and safe approach to template rendering. (Code is commented out and not active.)

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user-controlled search_query parameter directly into SQL: s_query = f"SELECT filename FROM files WHERE user_id = {user_id} AND filename LIKE '%{search_query}%'". The search_query comes from request.args.get('search') with no sanitization.

Reflected XSS via the search parameter. The template renders search_query with the | safe filter: value="{{ search_query | safe }}", which disables Jinja2 auto-escaping. An attacker can inject JavaScript via the search GET parameter on /dashboard.

Stored XSS via the country field. The profile template renders user.country with the | safe filter: {{ user.country | safe }}, disabling auto-escaping. An attacker can set their country to a script payload via the edit profile form, which executes when any user views their profile.

DOM-based XSS in the comment submission JavaScript. User input from the comment input field is appended directly to the DOM as HTML: $commentList.append('
  • ' + comment + '
    • '). No sanitization or encoding is applied, allowing script injection via comment content.

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY: SECRET_KEY = "just_another_secret". This key is used to sign session cookies and JWT tokens. An attacker who knows this key can forge session cookies to impersonate any user and forge JWT tokens.
Passwords are hashed using MD5 (hashlib.md5) with no salt. MD5 is cryptographically broken and trivially reversible via rainbow tables. The function is used for all password storage and verification.

Flask debug mode is enabled in production config: DEBUG = True. This exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which can leak source code, environment variables, and allows arbitrary code execution via the debugger console.

Session cookie HttpOnly flag is explicitly disabled: SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = False. This allows client-side JavaScript to access the session cookie, making session hijacking via XSS attacks trivial (and XSS is present in the app).

No CSRF protection on any form in the application. Flask-WTF is not used and no CSRF tokens are generated or validated. The update_profile endpoint is the most critical: a CSRF attack could change a victim's role to admin, escalating privileges. All POST forms (login, signup, update_profile, upload, delete) are vulnerable.

BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) on the API profile endpoint. The @token_required decorator is commented out (line 152-153), so /api/v1/profile?user_id=X returns any user's profile (username, email, country, role, permissions, team) without any authentication. An attacker can enumerate all user profiles.

BFLA (Broken Function Level Authorization) on the delete-user API endpoint. The @token_required decorator is commented out (lines 221-222), so DELETE /api/v1/delete-user/<user_id> can be called by anyone without authentication to delete any user from the database.

BOPA (Broken Object Property Level Authorization) / Mass Assignment allowing privilege escalation. The update_profile endpoint accepts 'role' and 'permissions' fields from the POST form body (lines 187-196). Although these fields are commented out in the HTML form, an attacker can add role=admin&permissions=all to the POST request to escalate to admin privileges.

Unrestricted file upload with no validation on file type, extension, size, or content. The upload endpoint accepts any file and saves it directly using the user-provided filename. An attacker could upload executable files, web shells, or malicious content.

Path traversal in file upload. The original filename from the upload is used directly without sanitization: filename = file.filename, then filepath = os.path.join(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename). A crafted filename like '../../evil.py' would write the file outside the intended upload directory, potentially overwriting application files.

SSRF in the update_picture API endpoint. The server fetches a user-supplied URL via requests.get(picture_url) with no validation or restriction on the URL scheme, host, or port. An attacker can make the server send requests to internal services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/ for cloud metadata, internal APIs, or localhost services).

No brute-force protection on the login endpoint. The /login route accepts unlimited authentication attempts with no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or delay mechanism. An attacker can perform credential stuffing or brute-force attacks against user accounts.

JWT tokens are signed with the hardcoded weak secret 'just_another_secret' from Config.SECRET_KEY. An attacker who knows this secret can forge valid JWT tokens to impersonate any user on the API, bypassing authentication entirely.

Missing authentication on profile pictures endpoint. The /uploads/profile_pictures/<filename> route serves profile pictures to anyone without requiring login. An attacker can enumerate and access all user profile pictures by iterating over numeric IDs (1.png, 2.png, etc.).

Error message printed to console on signup failure: print('Error inserting user:', e). In debug mode (which is enabled), this could expose database error details including table structure and SQL errors to the console/logs.

Exception details returned to user in SSRF endpoint error handling: return {'message': str(e)}, 500. This leaks internal error messages, stack traces, and potentially internal network information (hostname resolution errors, connection refused on internal ports, etc.) to the attacker.

Database seeding script hardcodes credentials for user 'bob_brown' with password 'my-secret' and 'write' permissions. This is distinct from the hardcoded SECRET_KEY (threatbyte-005) and JWT secret (threatbyte-017) — those are application secrets, while this is a seeded user account with a known weak password. If the seed data is loaded in any deployed environment, an attacker with source code knowledge can authenticate as bob_brown with write-level access.

The API login endpoint POST /api/v1/login has no rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection. This is a separate attack surface from the web login at /login (covered by threatbyte-016 in server/routes.py). Protecting the web login route does not protect the API login route — they are independent Flask route handlers in separate files. An attacker can perform unlimited credential brute-force attempts against the API endpoint.

The CI workflow downloads the OpenGrep binary via curl from a GitHub release URL (https://github.com/opengrep/opengrep/releases/download/v1.3.0/opengrep_manylinux_x86) without any checksum or signature verification. The downloaded binary is then executed with full access to the repository contents and CI secrets. If the opengrep release is compromised (via supply chain attack, account takeover, or DNS hijacking), a malicious binary would execute in the CI pipeline.

The ZAP DAST baseline scan is run with the -I flag (line 53: '-a -I'), which forces ZAP to return exit code 0 regardless of security findings. This means the CI pipeline will never fail due to DAST results — XSS, SQL injection, and other dynamic findings are silently ignored, allowing vulnerable code to be merged and deployed without any gate.

Login query uses parameterized query with ? placeholders: cursor.execute(query, (username, username)). Despite user input being passed to the query, it is safely parameterized and not vulnerable to SQL injection.
Signup INSERT query uses parameterized query with ? placeholders: cursor.execute(query, (username, email, country, hashed_password)). User-supplied values are safely parameterized.

Dashboard file listing query (when no search term) uses parameterized query: cursor.execute('SELECT filename FROM files WHERE user_id = ?', (user_id,)). This is the safe code path contrasting with the vulnerable search path on lines 137-138.
API login query uses parameterized query: cursor.execute(query, (username, username)) with query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? OR email = ?'. User input is safely parameterized.

File download via send_from_directory(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename) is NOT vulnerable to path traversal. Flask's send_from_directory() safely resolves the path and raises a 404 if the resolved path is outside the specified directory, preventing directory traversal attacks.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of unsanitized username path parameter into raw SQL query: user_query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'" followed by db.session.execute(text(user_query)). Reachable from GET /users/v1/{username} without authentication.

Unauthorized password change (IDOR). When vuln=1, the update_password function uses the username from the URL path parameter to look up the user whose password to change, instead of using the authenticated user from the JWT token (resp['sub']). Any authenticated user can change any other user's password by sending PUT /users/v1/{victim_username}/password.

Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA). When vuln=1, get_by_title queries the book by title only (Book.query.filter_by(book_title=str(book_title)).first()) without verifying the authenticated user is the owner. Any authenticated user can read any book's secret_content by sending GET /books/v1/{book_title}.

Mass assignment vulnerability allowing privilege escalation. When vuln=1, the register_user function checks if 'admin' is present in the user-supplied JSON body and uses it to set the admin flag on the new user. An attacker can register as admin by including '"admin": true' in the POST /users/v1/register request body.

Excessive data exposure through unauthenticated debug endpoint. GET /users/v1/_debug returns all user details including plaintext passwords, email addresses, and admin status for every user via User.get_all_users_debug(). No authentication or authorization is required.

User and password enumeration via differential error messages. When vuln=1, login_user returns 'Password is not correct for the given username.' for valid usernames with wrong passwords (line 103) and 'Username does not exist' for invalid usernames (line 106). This allows attackers to enumerate valid usernames.

Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS). When vuln=1, update_email uses a complex regex with nested quantifiers: r"^([0-9a-zA-Z]([-.\.\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])*@{1}([0-9a-zA-Z][-\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z]\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,9})$". The nested groups ([-.\.\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])* cause catastrophic backtracking with crafted input, consuming excessive CPU.

attack_chain: POST /users/v1/login — authenticate and obtain JWT token
PUT /users/v1/{username}/email with body {"email": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!"} — triggers catastrophic backtracking
poc.notes: Execution time doubles per additional character. 30 'a' + '!' = 21.6s server-side. No input length validation or regex timeout protects the endpoint.

description: JWT authentication bypass via weak/hardcoded signing key. The SECRET_KEY used for signing and verifying JWT tokens is hardcoded as the string 'random' (config.py line 13). An attacker who knows this trivially guessable key can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including admin accounts, achieving complete authentication bypass.

Flask application runs with debug=True (vuln_app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, debug=True)). This enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger which exposes detailed stack traces with local variable values on errors and may allow arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is compromised.

Lack of resources and rate limiting. All API endpoints are registered (vuln_app.add_api('openapi3.yml')) without any rate-limiting middleware or throttling mechanism. This allows unlimited requests to authentication endpoints (login, register) enabling brute-force attacks, and unlimited requests to all other endpoints enabling denial of service. No Flask-Limiter or equivalent is used.

The populate_db() function, exposed as the /createdb endpoint, drops and recreates all database tables and populates them with default data without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated attacker can call this endpoint to wipe the entire database, causing complete data loss and denial of service. Data flow: Unauthenticated HTTP request → /createdb route → populate_db() → SQLAlchemy db.drop_all() + db.create_all() + seeded inserts. No auth check at any point in the chain.

The init_db_users() function creates users with hardcoded, trivially guessable credentials: name1/pass1, name2/pass2, and admin/pass1. These default credentials are publicly visible in the source code and will be present after any database reset via /createdb. Any attacker can log in as any user, including the admin account, using these publicly known default credentials. Distinct from vampi-008 which covers the hardcoded JWT SECRET_KEY in config.py — this finding covers hardcoded user account passwords.

The get_all_users() function at lines 19-21 implements a GET /users/v1/ endpoint that returns all registered usernames and email addresses with no authentication check. Any unauthenticated attacker can enumerate all user accounts and email addresses in a single request, enabling targeted phishing and credential stuffing. Distinct from vampi-005 (the /users/v1/_debug endpoint at lines 24-26 which also exposes plaintext passwords) — this is a different function exposing a subset of user data through the regular user listing endpoint.

Safe parameterized ORM query. User.query.filter_by(username=request_data.get('username')).first() uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by which automatically parameterizes the query, preventing SQL injection. The username from user input is safely bound as a parameter.
